cards.explanation: The answer is the evil they had done. The LORD says the ruins are "…because of the evil they have done." They provoked Him by burning incense and serving other gods (Jeremiah 44:3). The ruins have a reason, friends, and He names it plainly.

The answer is False. The LORD says these gods were ones "…that neither they nor you nor your fathers ever knew." Nobody in the family tree had a history with them. That's a lot of incense for a stranger.

The answer is False. The prophets warned again and again, and the people did not listen. They did not turn from their wickedness or stop burning incense to other gods (Jeremiah 44:5). Warning after warning, same smoke, friends.

The answer is wrath. The LORD says, "Therefore My wrath and anger poured out and burned in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem…" It's strong language, and the text means it. That's how those cities became the ruins the people could see for themselves.

The answer is an object of cursing and reproach. The LORD says that as a result, "…you will be cut off and will become an object of cursing and reproach among all the nations of the earth." That's the outcome He names for burning incense to other gods in Egypt. Nobody wants a reputation like that, friends.

The answer is False. The LORD says, "To this day they have not humbled themselves or shown reverence…" They also haven't followed His instruction or the statutes He set before them. Humbling themselves was the one thing still not on the list, friends.

The answer is by sword or famine. The LORD says, "They will all fall by the sword or be consumed by famine." Then He says it again for emphasis: "From the least to the greatest, they will die by sword or famine…" That sentence reaches from the least to the greatest, bakers.

The answer is True. The LORD says, "I will punish those who live in the land of Egypt, just as I punished Jerusalem, by sword and famine and plague…" Notice that plague joins the list here. The people who left Jerusalem behind were not leaving the warning behind, friends.
The answer is only a few fugitives. The LORD says "…none will return except a few fugitives." They long to go back to Judah, and only a few will make it. That's the sting of the verse, bakers.
The answer is "We will not listen to you." The assembly tells Jeremiah, the prophet, "…we will not listen to you!" It's a no from a great assembly, friends.

The answer is plenty of food and no disaster. The people say, "At that time we had plenty of food and good things, and we saw no disaster." Keep in mind that this is their own account of it. They're the ones giving the reason, and Jeremiah answers them next.

The answer is True, that's what they say. They tell Jeremiah, "…from the time we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine." Remember, friends, it's their claim. Jeremiah has a different answer coming.

The answer is remember. Jeremiah asks, "…did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind?" It's a question with an answer built right in. The incense in Judah's cities did not slip past the LORD, friends.

The answer is False. Jeremiah says, "Because you burned incense and sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD…" The disaster is tied to the burning, not to stopping. He turns their whole argument around, bakers.

The answer is invoke His name. The LORD says, "I have sworn by My great name… that never again will any man of Judah living in the land of Egypt invoke My name or say, 'As surely as the Lord GOD lives.'" It's a serious oath, and He swears it by His own great name, friends.

The answer is False. The LORD says, "I am watching over them for harm and not for good…" He then says every man of Judah in Egypt will meet his end by sword or famine. It's a heavy verse, friends, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.
The answer is word. The LORD says the whole remnant "…will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs!" The question on the table was whose word holds up. They'll find out, bakers.

The answer is that he will be handed to his enemies. The LORD says, "…I will deliver Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hands of his enemies who seek his life…" Pharaoh Hophra is the king of the very land these people went to. That land has a king with trouble of his own. And friends, this is the last passage in this group, so that closes out the story of the fall of Jerusalem and the remnant.
